stem:
A 62-year-old man is being evaluated for shortness of breath.  During pulmonary function testing, the patient performs a forceful and complete exhalation after maximal inhalation.  His results (red curve) are compared to a healthy individual of the same age and sex (black curve), as shown in the image below:

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's dyspnea?​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌

options.label: E
options.text: Unable to determine without bronchodilator testing

explanation:
Spirometry is a component of pulmonary function testing (PFT).  During spirometry, the patient completely inhales to reach total lung capacity, and then forcefully exhales as much air as possible as quickly as possible.  The volume of exhaled air is measured as a function of time.  The volume expelled during the first second of exhalation is the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1).  The total volume of air expelled represents the forced vital capacity (FVC).

The black curve on the graph depicts a normal spirometry tracing from a healthy individual, with FEV1 = 4 liters, an FVC = 5 liters, yielding an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.8.  The patient's red curve shows a reduced FEV1 = 2.75 liters and a reduced FVC = 3 liters, giving an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.92.

A restrictive process should be suspected when FEV1 and FVC are both decreased and airflow obstruction is absent (ie, an FEV1/FVC >0.7).  Therefore, this patient's results are most consistent with interstitial lung disease (eg, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis).

(Choices A, B and E)  Asthma (during active bronchoconstriction) and emphysema both demonstrate an obstructive pattern on spirometry with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (≤0.7).  In this situation, bronchodilator testing can differentiate between the two conditions; airflow obstruction due to asthma is reversible, whereas obstruction due to emphysema is not.  Because asthma involves intermittent bronchospasm, spirometry is typically normal between acute exacerbations.

(Choice D)  Pulmonary arterial hypertension can cause dyspnea.  However, it involves the pulmonary vessels rather than the airways or lung parenchyma, so airflow (ie, spirometry) and lung volumes are usually normal despite evidence of impaired gas transfer (ie, reduced diffusing capacity).

Educational objective:Spirometry measures the volume of air that can be forcefully exhaled over time.  Key values include the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and the total volume of air that can be exhaled (FVC).  A restrictive processes should be suspected when FEV1 and FVC are both decreased and obstruction is absent (ie, normal FEV1/FVC ratio).​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌
